newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Germany isolated as EU debates Euro stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Germany isolated as EU debates Euro stability pact.

text.p: Germany was isolated on Thursday at an 11th-hour meeting of European Union finance ministers called to clinch an elusive deal to ensure strict budget discipline under a future single currency.

EU diplomats said that during an initial round of talks on the eve of an EU summit countries had kept to their previous positions, leaving Bonn isolated in its demands for emphatic rules against countries running excessive deficits.
Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson, arriving for what he predicted would be dramatic talks, said the issue of the stbility pact may well have to be handed over to EU leaders to sort out on Friday.
Irish Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn also threw cold water on the idea of a quick deal before the summit.
"I have no prior indication that we can anticipate a breakthrough," Quinn said.
At issue is Germany's insistence that countries in a single currency bloc should be fined for excessive budget deficits and that there should be only clearly defined exceptions.
The German government is determined to ensure that the economic framework for the euro is strict enough to produce a single European currency which is a robust as the German mark.
Bonn's partners want greater flexibility and are asking Germany to make it easier for offending nations to avoid sanctions if their economies are in trouble.
But German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who dreamt up the idea of the stability pact, remained firm on Thursday.
Although he said on his arrival in Dublin he was prepared to seek a "good solution", he had earlier told the Bonn parliament, "I will not move away from the clear stability goal."
Financial markets will be watching the talks closely, keen to see whether the single currency project is still on track.
Any indication that the stability pact is being watered down could lead to pressure on the German mark.

Germany's current proposals envisage nations being exempt from fines for excessive budget deficits if their economies contract over 12 successive months. The size of the contraction is what the ministers were knocking heads over.
The stability pact is a key element of a report on economic and monetary union (EMU) due to be studied by EU leaders at the summit proper, which begins on Friday.

Other aspects of the report have already been informally agreed. They include the legal basis for the euro and a new post-EMU exchange rate mechanism to keep EU currencies outside the euro bloc stable.
The EU leaders were also to discuss at the summit the bloc's long-term future, in the shape of a draft EU treaty written by the Irish EU presidency.

"We posed ourselves several ambitious but realistic challenges in key areas relevant to the concerns of people in Europe in 1996," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said. "We believe we have realised our ambitions in all areas."

The Irish draft treaty shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.
It also calls for the EU to create by 2001 a vast area of freedom, security and justice that ensures the free movement of people.

Of all the leaders coming to Dublin, British Prime Minister John Major will be among the most watched. With his ruling Conservative party torn apart over Europe, Major will be under pressure not to appear too conciliatory to his EU colleagues.
Britain opposes most of the proposals under discussion for the draft treaty -- which is supposed to prepare the bloc for enlargement into central and eastern Europe.
London also has an opt-out on the single currency, making discussions on post-EMU life something of a political minefield for the embattled British leader.
